intro: Every rule needs explaining. The Torah says rest on Shabbat, but it does not say what rest means. It says dwell in booths, but not how tall a booth should be. For hundreds of years, Jewish teachers passed explanations from one person to the next, out loud, by memory. Rabbinic tradition calls this the Oral Torah.

This unit follows that chain from Mount Sinai to a book. You will meet Ezra reading the Torah to a crowd, the Pharisees and Sadducees arguing about tradition, and Hillel and Shammai, who disagreed and are both remembered. Then you will watch a city burn, a rabbi escape in a coffin, and a scholar named Judah the Prince gather everything into the Mishnah.

By the end, you will be able to tell the Written Torah from the Oral Torah, name the six orders of the Mishnah, and explain why the rabbis kept the opinions that lost. You will also practice the course's habit: say who holds a belief, and describe what a text says without deciding whether it is true.
bigQuestion: How did the Oral Torah travel from memory to the Mishnah, and why did the rabbis write it down?

timeline.t: Jewish tradition places Moses at Mount Sinai around this time; historians debate the date
The Babylonians destroy the First Temple in Jerusalem and take many Jews into exile
The Second Temple is finished after the return from Babylon
Ezra reads the Torah aloud in Jerusalem while helpers explain it (Nehemiah 8)
Hillel and Shammai teach in Jerusalem; the Pharisees and Sadducees disagree about the Oral Torah
Rome destroys the Second Temple; Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai teaches at Yavneh
The Bar Kokhba revolt fails; tradition says Rabbi Akiva is put to death; rabbis move to the Galilee
Rabbi Judah the Prince gathers the Oral Torah into the Mishnah: six orders, 63 tractates
The Gemara of the Land of Israel is gathered into the Jerusalem Talmud
The Babylonian Talmud takes shape; Mishnah plus Gemara equals Talmud

words.d: the first five books of the Hebrew Bible; the word means teaching

a teaching or practice handed down from one generation to the next
the scribe who, the Bible says, read the Torah aloud in Jerusalem, c. 450 BCE
in rabbinic tradition, a council of teachers after Ezra, a link in the chain
a Second Temple group that accepted the traditions of the elders, the Oral Torah
a Second Temple group, many of them priests, that accepted only the Written Torah
a patient teacher around the end of the first century BCE, paired with Shammai
the town where the rabbis rebuilt Jewish teaching after the Temple fell in 70 CE

test.q: What are the five books of the Written Torah?
choices: Seeds, Festivals, Women, Damages, Holy Things
test.why: The Written Torah is Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. The first list is Mishnah orders; the second is tractates.

test.q: In rabbinic tradition, how was the Oral Torah passed on before it was written?
choices: spoken by a teacher and remembered by a student
test.why: The Oral Torah, tradition holds, was passed by memory from teacher to student for many generations.

test.q: Which text begins with Moses receiving the Torah and handing it to Joshua?
test.why: Pirkei Avot 1:1 lists the chain: Moses, Joshua, the elders, the prophets, the Men of the Great Assembly.

test.q: What did Ezra's helpers do in Nehemiah 8?
choices: They gave the sense so the people understood the reading
test.why: Nehemiah 8:8 says they read clearly and gave the sense so that the people understood.

test.q: Why does a rule like no work on Shabbat need explaining?
choices: It does not say what counts as work
test.why: The Torah gives the rule but not a list of what work means. The Mishnah in tractate Shabbat lists thirty-nine kinds.

test.q: Which group rejected the Oral Torah?
test.why: The Sadducees accepted only the Written Torah. The Pharisees, and the rabbis after them, accepted the traditions of the elders.

test.q: What is a fence around the Torah?
choices: the outer text on a Talmud page
the poles of a Torah scroll
an extra rule that keeps a person from breaking a Torah rule
test.why: The Men of the Great Assembly, in Avot 1:1, taught to make a fence around the Torah: a guarding rule.
In 70 CE the Roman army burned the Second Temple. Babylon destroyed the First Temple in 586 BCE; the Mishnah is c. 200 CE.

test.q: What did Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai ask Vespasian for, in the Talmud's story?
test.why: Gittin 56b tells that he asked for Yavneh and its sages, Rabban Gamliel's family, and a doctor for Rabbi Zadok.

test.q: Why did the rabbis gather the Oral Torah into a book?
choices: They feared it would be forgotten as teachers died
test.why: After the wars with Rome killed many teachers, the rabbis feared the memorized teachings would be lost.

test.q: Who is called Rabbi in the Talmud?
test.why: The Talmud calls Judah the Prince, who gathered the Mishnah c. 200 CE, simply Rabbi.

test.q: How many orders and tractates does the Mishnah have?
test.why: The Mishnah has six orders holding sixty-three tractates.

test.q: In what language is the Mishnah written?
test.why: The Mishnah is in short, clear Hebrew. Most of the Gemara is in Aramaic.

test.q: Which sentence describes the Mishnah's style?
test.why: The Mishnah states rules in short sentences and often records who disagreed, without giving reasons.

test.q: What do the Mishnah and the Gemara make together?
test.why: The Talmud is the Mishnah plus the Gemara, the rabbis' discussion of it.

write.prompt: Why did the rabbis keep more than one answer to a question? Use Mishnah Berakhot 1:1 and Mishnah Sukkah 1:1, and one more passage from the unit if you like. Tell what each passage says, then explain how the rabbis of the Mishnah and today's readers understand keeping the losing side.
tips: Name each passage: the tractate and the chapter and mishnah, like Berakhot 1:1.
Say who holds each belief: rabbinic tradition holds, the Mishnah says, historians think.
Describe what the text does; do not say whether it is true.
Use the unit's words: Oral Torah, Mishnah, tractate, disagreement.
